excerpt: When a photograph or a voice can be manufactured: the checks that still work, the family code word, and the rule about money and urgency.

body.text: This lesson is about pictures and voices that can be faked. You will learn how a fake image or a copied voice is made, the checks that still work, and the family code word that settles a panicked call.
A photograph used to be evidence. A voice on the phone used to be proof of who was speaking. Both are now easy to copy, and the checks have moved from the picture to the conversation around it.
Before you start

items: About twenty minutes.
One family member to agree a code word with.
A second way to reach the people who matter.

body.text: How the fakes work

items: An image can be generated from a written description, in any style.
A face can be placed on another person's head in a video.
A voice can be copied from a few seconds of recording.
A message can be written in a relative's style after reading their posts.
A profile can be copied, with the same name and photograph.
All of it is cheap, fast, and improving every year.

body.text: You will see a photograph that looks slightly too smooth, with strange hands or jewellery that melts into the skin. Those details are clues, and none of them is proof, so the checks below matter more than the clues.

body.alt: A printed photograph compared with the same image on a phone.
body.caption: A print and a screen, side by side. Compare an image with the original rather than judging it alone.

body.text: It looks like a clear picture must be real. A clear picture is the norm now, and the deciding question is who sent it and why.
The checks that work

items: Call the person back on a number you already have, not the one in the message.
Ask a question only they could answer, such as the name of a shared neighbour.
Send the picture to somebody who was there, and ask when it was taken.
Search the image itself, which finds the older original when it exists.
Slow down: every fake needs urgency, and every real emergency survives five minutes.
Refuse to send money on the strength of one message, however convincing.

body.text: A reverse image search will show a results page with the same picture on older pages, sometimes years old. When the same face appears in five countries, the picture is not evidence of anything.

body.alt: An older man listening carefully during a phone call.
body.caption: The hardest calls target the people who care most. A code word protects them without insulting them.

body.text: The family code word
Agree one word, known to the family and useless to anybody else.

items: Choose a word that is not on anybody's social media.
Teach it to the people who might be impersonated, not only the ones who worry.
Use it when a call asks for money, and use it calmly.
Change it if it has been shared outside the family.
Write it in the notebook the family keeps, in a sealed page if you prefer.
Practice once, so the word comes to mind when the call is frightening.

body.text: None of this needs special software. A call back on a known number, one question, and five minutes of patience stop most of these attacks.
Do not worry about seeming suspicious. The people who love you would rather be asked a question than send money to a stranger.
If it goes wrong
Every case here has a next step, and speed beats shame every time.

items: You sent money: report it to the bank at once, and keep every message.
You gave a code: change it immediately, in the app where it is used.
A relative's account is copied: report the profile, and tell the real person.
You shared a picture that is now being reused: tell the people who trust you.
A video looks real and frightens you: check the original source before reacting.
You feel foolish: that feeling is the tool the attacker used, and naming it helps.

body.text: Practice
Agree one code word this week.

items: Choose a word the family will remember.
Tell two people about it, face to face.
Practise one pretend call with the word.
Write it in the family notebook.
Agree the rule: money requests are always checked by a call back.

body.text: You can now hear a convincing lie and still check it. In the next lesson you will keep your own judgment in a world of recommendations.

excerpt: Feeds, recommendations, and notifications that decide for you: how to notice the nudge, and the small habits that keep the choosing.

body.text: This lesson keeps your judgment yours. You will learn how recommendation feeds decide what you see, how notifications borrow your attention, and the small habits that put the choosing back in your hands.
A feed is sorted by what keeps you watching, not by what is true or useful. That sorting is useful sometimes and costly often, and noticing it is the first skill.
Before you start

items: One phone, and ten minutes.
A notebook for two observations.
Willingness to change one setting.

body.text: How the choosing moves

items: The feed shows what held other people's attention longest.
Adverts are placed by the same logic, between the things you wanted.
Autoplay decides that the next video should start without asking.
A notification arrives at the hour you usually open the app.
A shop's page arranges choices so the first option wins.
None of this is a conspiracy, and all of it shapes a decision.

body.text: You will see the same three videos again after you watch one of them, and the repetition is the system learning rather than a coincidence. Watching one more teaches it to send twenty more.

body.alt: Hands writing in a notebook with no computer nearby.
body.caption: A page and a pen, with no feed attached. Some thinking needs the noise switched off.

body.text: It looks like you chose what to watch. You choose within a list somebody else arranged, and knowing that changes how much of the list you accept.
Taking the choosing back

items: Turn off autoplay in the apps you use most.
Set notifications to arrive in batches, or turn most of them off.
Search for what you want instead of scrolling what arrives.
Give a decision an hour before buying anything advertised to you.
Write a short list before you open a shop's page, and buy from the list.
Check one important decision against a person rather than a feed.

body.text: The settings page will show a list of switches for notifications, and each one is a decision somebody made for you. Turning three off is a five-minute job with a quiet week afterwards.

body.alt: A clock beside a hand writing on paper.
body.caption: An hour between the advert and the purchase. Most urges do not survive it.

body.text: Thinking without a screen

items: Write the decision on paper before looking anything up.
Say the reasons aloud, which exposes the weak ones.
Ask what you would choose if nobody were watching.
Sleep on anything that costs more than a day's pay.
Keep one hour a day with no feed, even if it is only the walk home.
Judge a week by what you did, not by what you watched.

body.text: None of this needs an expensive course or a new phone. Three switches, one list, and an hour of silence change more than any productivity app.
Do not worry about being manipulated by everything. You are allowed to enjoy a feed, and you are allowed to know when you are being steered.
If it goes wrong
Every case here has a correction, and none of them requires leaving the internet.

items: You spent an evening scrolling: note the time, and set one switch tonight.
You bought something unplanned: return it, or write the reason you kept it.
The app shows upsetting content: report it once, and stop watching it.
You cannot concentrate on a book: read ten pages before opening the phone.
You feel behind after scrolling: that feeling is the product working.
You keep comparing your life: unfollow the accounts that do it, by name.

body.text: Practice
Change three settings and keep a small record.

items: Turn off autoplay in two apps.
Turn off all but three notifications.
Write a shopping list before opening any shop.
Spend one hour without a feed today.
Write what you noticed in the notebook.

body.text: You can now keep your own counsel in a noisy place. In the next lesson you will learn anything faster than you expect.

excerpt: A practice loop that actually works: small sessions, spaced repetition, teaching it back, and a first project small enough to finish.

body.text: This lesson is about learning faster than you expect. You will learn a practice loop that fits a busy week, why spacing beats cramming, and how a small finished project teaches more than a long course.
Learning happens when you try, fail, and try again with attention. Watching somebody else do it feels like learning and leaves very little behind.
Before you start

items: One skill you want, named plainly.
Thirty minutes a day for two weeks.
A notebook and a pen.

body.text: The loop

items: Watch or read one small piece, then stop.
Do it yourself straight away, with the material closed.
Compare your attempt with the example.
Write the mistake in one line.
Repeat the same piece tomorrow before adding anything new.
Review the mistakes once a week.

body.text: You will see the second attempt improve without any new teaching, and that improvement is the loop working. Doing beats watching at every stage.

body.alt: A study plan chart pinned on a wall.
body.caption: A small plan on a wall. Six weeks of thirty minutes beats one heroic weekend.

body.text: It looks like a long course teaches more than a short practice. A finished small project teaches more than a finished long video, because the project makes you decide.
Spacing and recall

items: Learn a piece, then leave it for a day.
Recall it from memory before opening the notes.
Review after two days, then after a week.
Write questions for yourself, and answer them without looking.
Mix old material with new, instead of finishing one topic completely.
Keep the sessions short enough to repeat tomorrow.

body.text: A page of your own questions will show which ideas survive a night and which do not. The ones that vanish are the ones to review, and the rest can wait.
You will see those questions on the page when you open your notes, and the ones you cannot answer are tomorrow's work. A page of questions is a better study plan than a page of highlights.

body.alt: A student pausing a video lesson to take notes.
body.caption: Pause, write, then play. A paused video is a lesson, and a playing one is a broadcast.

body.text: Teach it back
Explaining a thing out loud finds the gaps faster than reading it again.

items: Explain the topic to somebody who does not know it.
Use your own examples, not the ones in the video.
Notice the moment you reach for a word you cannot define.
Write that word down, and learn it next.
Explain it again the following week.
Keep the explanation short, under two minutes.

body.text: A short first project is the test of the loop. Choose something you can finish in a week, such as one page, one short interview, or one small repair, and finish it before starting anything larger.
None of this needs a paid course. A notebook, thirty minutes, and one person who will listen cover the whole method.
Do not worry about learning slowly. Most people who seem quick are repeating the same small loop, and the loop is available to you today.
If it goes wrong
Every case here has a fix, and none of it is about talent.

items: You miss a week: start again with the smallest session, not the biggest.
You forget everything: the spacing was too long, so review sooner.
You are bored: the piece is too large, so cut it in half.
You are busy: do ten minutes rather than nothing, and mark the calendar.
You cannot find a project: build the smallest useful version of the thing.
You compare yourself with others: compare with your attempt last week.

body.text: Practice
Run the loop for one week on one skill.

items: Name the skill in one line.
Choose the smallest first piece.
Do it with the material closed.
Write yesterday's mistake before today's practice.
Explain the week's work to somebody on Sunday.

body.text: You can now learn on purpose rather than by accident. In the next lesson you will look at the work that changes and the work that stays.

excerpt: What machines take, what they leave, and how to keep your skills portable when the job description shifts under your feet.

body.text: This lesson is about the work that changes and the work that stays. You will learn which tasks machines are taking, which parts of a job remain human, and how to keep your skills portable when the description shifts.
Every trade has a part that can be written down and a part that cannot. The written part moves to software first, and the rest stays with the person who can be trusted.
Before you start

items: A list of what your week actually contains.
About twenty minutes.
A notebook for two columns.

body.text: What moves first

items: Repeating the same form with different names.
Copying numbers from one place to another.
Writing the same letter with a new date.
Summarising a long document that follows a pattern.
Answering the same five questions all day.
Checking whether a page has every required field.

body.text: You will see a task disappear into a template or a chat window, and the time it frees is real. What you do with that time decides whether the change helps you.

body.alt: A worker writing in a notebook beside a laptop.
body.caption: Two columns: what a machine can do, and what needs a person. The second list is your work.

body.text: It looks like automation removes a whole job. Most changes remove tasks, and the job that remains is the part customers were always paying for.
What stays human

items: Deciding what should be done at all.
Taking responsibility when something fails.
Reading a room, a customer, or a worry that is not written down.
Handling money, keys, and access, where trust is the product.
Fixing the physical thing, with hands and a screwdriver.
Teaching somebody else, which needs patience rather than knowledge alone.

body.text: A customer will still ask for the person who answered last time, and that request is the clearest sign of what a machine cannot replace.
You will see a chat window answer a question in a second, and nobody asks it for the name of the person who helped. The name is what customers come back for.
A job advert will appear with a list of tools, and the same advert will ask for somebody who can be trusted with the keys. The second line is the one that keeps the job human.

body.alt: Rows of desks in a computer room with people working.
body.caption: The same room, different tasks. Skills move with the person, and desks move with the work.

body.text: Keeping skills portable

items: Write down three things you do that a customer would pay for on their own.
Learn the tool that removes your least favourite task.
Keep a folder of finished work you can show somebody.
Learn to explain what you do in one sentence.
Ask one person in a different trade what they need help with.
Review the plan every six months, since the tools move.

body.text: None of this needs a career change. One new tool and one plain sentence about your value carry more than a certificate nobody asked for.
Do not worry about the pace of change. Most of it arrives slowly, and the people who keep learning a little are rarely caught out.
If it goes wrong
Every case here has a step, and none of them starts with panic.

items: A tool does your main task: learn to run the tool, and keep the judgment.
Work slows for a month: call past customers, and ask what they need now.
Your employer changes systems: be the person who learns it first.
A certificate expires: note the date, and renew before it lapses.
A skill is not selling: ask three buyers what they would pay for.
You feel too old to start: the first lesson takes thirty minutes.

body.text: Practice
Draw the two columns for your own week.

items: List every task in a normal week.
Mark the ones a machine could repeat.
Mark the ones that need judgment or trust.
Choose one task from the first list and learn its tool.
Choose one from the second and get better at it on purpose.

body.text: You can now see your own work clearly. There is one lesson left, and it is about the road ahead.

excerpt: The last lesson: what to keep from ten chapters, the notebook that holds it together, and the next step that is small enough to take today.

body.text: This is the last lesson in the course, and it is about what comes next. You will look back at what you have learned, keep the habits that matter, and choose a next step small enough to take today.
Two hundred and ten lessons are a lot of ground. What stays is not the whole of it, and the parts that stay will be the ones you used.
Before you start

items: Your notebook, if you have kept one.
Twenty minutes, with the phone face down.
One honest question: what do I want to do next?

body.text: What to keep

items: The habit of writing a fault down before touching the machine.
The five questions, in order, for anything that stops working.
The backup you made, and the date you checked it.
The password notebook, kept away from the router.
One plain sentence that explains what you can do for somebody.
The knowledge that a confusing screen is normal before it is understood.

body.text: You will see your notebook fill differently now, with dates, prices, and the words people used rather than the words the manual used. That handwriting is the course, kept in a form you can carry.
The first page will show the date you started, and the last will show what you can do now. Reading both pages is the most honest measure of progress you will find.

body.alt: A view down an open road in the morning light.
body.caption: A road, a morning, and no hurry. The next step does not have to be large.

body.text: It looks like the end of a course should be a plan for years. A plan for this week is worth more, since this week is the one you can act on.
The three things worth doing

items: Fix one thing for somebody, free, and write down what you learned.
Back up one family machine, and check the copy.
Teach one person one lesson from this course.

body.text: The first of those three is how most support work begins. The second saves a family's photographs. The third is how you find out what you actually know.

body.alt: A computer on a desk with a notebook beside it.
body.caption: A desk, a machine, and a notebook. Most of this work begins at a table like this one.

body.text: When you feel behind
Everybody feels behind at some point, and the feeling is a poor guide to what you can do.

items: Compare with your own work from a month ago, not with somebody's best day.
Ask a question out loud, since most people are glad to answer.
Start with the smallest version of the thing you want to build.
Write down what you already finished, and read the list on a bad day.
Keep the notebook open, because the record answers the doubt.

body.text: None of this needs to be done alone. A group of two or three people learning the same thing moves faster than any of them would alone, and the meetings cost nothing but a table.
Do not worry about the parts you have forgotten. The lessons are here, and a page you have read before takes half the time on the second visit.
If it goes wrong
Every case here has a way forward, and each one is smaller than it looks.

items: You forget a procedure: open the lesson and follow the steps in order.
A machine defeats you: write the fault down, and ask one person who knows.
You lose the notebook: start a new one, and copy the last two entries.
A repair fails: say so early, and return the machine as you found it.
You feel like an impostor: show somebody the work you finished last month.
You have no customer yet: fix one thing for free and ask for a sentence in return.

body.text: Practice
Choose one step and do it this week.

items: Pick one of the three things above.
Write the day you will do it.
Tell one person you are doing it.
Do it, and write two lines afterwards.
Choose the next one only after the first is finished.

body.text: You have finished the course, and you know more than you did. The machine in front of you is a tool rather than a mystery, and the person using it is still the point.
